arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Elonis argued the First Amendment protects speech unless the speaker truly intends to threaten.
The government argued a reasonable person's interpretation proves the speaker intended a threat.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Elonis wants the conviction overturned because he did not truly intend to threaten.
The government wants the conviction upheld because a reasonable person would view the words as threats.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Elonis argues the First Amendment requires proof of the speaker's actual intent to threaten.
The government argues a reasonable person's interpretation of the words establishes the necessary intent.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor asked how a reasonable person's interpretation differs from the defendant's intent.
Chief Justice Roberts asked if online anger posts count as therapeutic rather than threatening.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the legal standard for prosecuting online speech as threats. It determines when words become criminal acts. It balances free expression against public safety. It sets a precedent for interpreting intent in digital communications.
